Well, if you ask Mary McGlynn she'll tell you that he told her flat-out, in English no less, "Dead.". Though it's not impossible that he gave more... diplomatic... answers to others, I'd take the answer he gave her as the definitive one.

I can't say I recall any cues that would indicate his survival, although I'd be interested in hearing what you have.

For my personal version, I base it on the fact that most of the time, when Spike's life is discussed, it is discussed in symbols and metaphor. Hell, in the first episode he states that he had "died" before. Thus, he was already on his second life. This isn't a new concept for the audience. A "second life" metaphorically means a dramatic change in one's life. That the end of the first life is marked by "death" is fitting, not surprising. What is different in Spike's case is that it becomes apparent he never truly concluded his old life, there is unfinished business that he has been running from (and that is a theme that extends to basically all of the Bebop's crew).

A particular symbol I like to bring up in regards to Spike's second life, is his Native American name: "Swimming Bird". Birds commonly are used as a symbol of the human spirit. However, Spike's spirit isn't flying... it's just treading water.

Spike isn't free to live his second life because he is still burdened by the remnants of the first. He claims that one of his eyes is always looking at the past. Releasing him from those burdens is what Vicious is referring to when he says that he is the only one that can "kill" Spike, not the literal "kill" which would make the statement illogical.

When Julia and Vicious are dead, Spike is finally freed from the stasis he was trapped in when he fled the Syndicate with unresolved issues between them all.

TL;DR - It's all open to interpretation, I suppose.
